---
title: "Two coupled neurons"
description: "Two spiking neurons wired to each other through synapses: why mutual inhibition makes them fire together, mutual excitation makes them alternate, and the synaptic time constant decides which."
toc: true
execute:
  enabled: false
---

Neurons in the cortex often fire in step with one another. Rhythms in the
gamma range, roughly 30 to 90 cycles per second (Buzsáki and Wang 2012), are
the best-known example, and they are a property of groups of cells, not of
any single one. The first guess about how neurons come to fire together is
that they excite each other. For these fast rhythms the guess turns out to
be wrong, or at least incomplete: in the models that reproduce gamma, the
inhibitory interneurons do the synchronising, and the excitatory
connections, if anything, pull the rhythm apart (Whittington, Traub and
Jefferys 1995; Buzsáki and Wang 2012). The smallest circuit that shows why
has just two neurons, and it was one of the exercises in the *Theoretical
Neuroscience* lecture at Goethe University Frankfurt, where I was a teaching
assistant. The exercise goes back to the courses of Thomas Burwick at the
same university, which I took as a student.

Everything runs in your browser. Pick a type for each neuron, set the two
coupling strengths, and watch the diagram, the two voltage traces, and the
phase between the two neurons update together.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// shared helpers: one persistent canvas per explorable, text-sized fonts, responsive width
exFont = ({size: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontSize, family: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily, toString() { return this.size + " " + this.family; }})
exFg = () => getComputedStyle(document.body).color
mkCanvas = (W, H) => {
  const c = DOM.context2d(W, H);
  c.canvas.style.width = "100%"; c.canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; c.canvas.style.height = "auto";
  return c;
}
axisBox = (c, x, y, w, h) => { c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeRect(x, y, w, h); }
```

## The model

Each neuron is the [leaky integrate-and-fire model](neuron.qmd) from the
first page, with the same numbers as in Dayan and Abbott (2001, section 5.8):
resting potential $E_L = -70$ mV, membrane time constant $\tau_m = 10$ ms, a
spike when the voltage reaches $-54$ mV, and a reset to $-80$ mV afterwards.
Both neurons receive the same constant drive $R_m I_e$, strong enough to
make each of them fire on its own. What is new is the synapse. A spike in
neuron $j$ opens channels in neuron $i$, and the current through them
depends on neuron $i$'s own voltage:

$$\tau_m \frac{dV_i}{dt} = E_L - V_i - g_{ji}\, P_j\, (V_i - E_{ji}) + R_m I_e .$$

Here $P_j$ is the fraction of open channels at the synapse made by neuron
$j$, $g_{ji}$ is the strength of that synapse, and $E_{ji}$ is its reversal
potential. The reversal potential is what makes a synapse excitatory or
inhibitory. With $E = 0$ mV the current always pushes the voltage up towards
threshold. With $E = -80$ mV it pushes it down, towards the reset. A neuron
that makes excitatory synapses is drawn as a triangle, after the pyramidal
cells of the cortex, and an inhibitory one as a circle, after the
interneurons. The strengths are dimensionless, in units where $g = 1$ means
the synaptic conductance at its peak equals the leak conductance.

After a spike, $P$ rises over a few milliseconds and then decays, with both
phases governed by one synaptic time constant $\tau_s$:

$$\tau_s \frac{dP}{dt} = e\, P_{\max}\, z\, (1 - P) - P, \qquad
\tau_s \frac{dz}{dt} = -z ,$$

where $z$ is set to 1 at every presynaptic spike and $P_{\max} = 0.5$. The
peak of $P$ comes about $\tau_s$ after the spike, which is the realistic
shape. The time constant turns out to matter as much as the sign.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cnType1 = Inputs.radio(new Map([["excitatory", 0], ["inhibitory", -80]]), {value: -80, label: "Neuron 1 (purple) makes synapses that are"})
viewof cnType2 = Inputs.radio(new Map([["excitatory", 0], ["inhibitory", -80]]), {value: -80, label: "Neuron 2 (teal) makes synapses that are"})
viewof cnG12 = Inputs.range([0, 0.6], {value: 0.2, step: 0.02, label: "Strength 1 → 2"})
viewof cnG21 = Inputs.range([0, 0.6], {value: 0.2, step: 0.02, label: "Strength 2 → 1"})
viewof cnTauS = Inputs.range([1, 30], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Synaptic time constant τₛ (ms)"})
viewof cnDrive = Inputs.range([17, 40], {value: 25, step: 1, label: "Drive RₘIₑ (mV)"})
viewof cnSpeed = Inputs.radio(new Map([["slow", 30], ["normal", 65], ["fast", 260]]), {value: 30, label: "Speed"})
viewof cnPause = Inputs.toggle({label: "Pause"})
viewof cnReset = Inputs.button("Reset with new random starting voltages")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
cnState = {
  cnReset;
  const dt = 0.05, EL = -70, Vth = -54, Vr = -80, taum = 10, Pmax = 0.5;
  const win = 200, n = Math.round(win / dt), phaseWin = 5000;
  const V = [Vr + (Vth - Vr) * Math.random(), Vr + (Vth - Vr) * Math.random()];
  const P = [0, 0], z = [0, 0];
  const trace = [new Float32Array(n).fill(V[0]), new Float32Array(n).fill(V[1])];
  const spikes = [[], []], phases = [];
  let t = 0, lastRate = [0, 0], nextRateAt = 1000, idx = 0;
  while (true) {
    if (!viewof cnPause.value) {
      const E = [viewof cnType1.value, viewof cnType2.value];           // reversal of synapses made by 1 and by 2
      const g = [viewof cnG21.value, viewof cnG12.value];               // g[i] = strength of the synapse onto neuron i
      const taus = viewof cnTauS.value, RI = viewof cnDrive.value;
      const stepsPerFrame = viewof cnSpeed.value;
      for (let s = 0; s < stepsPerFrame; s++) {
        idx = (idx + 1) % n;
        const dV = [0, 0];
        for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) { const j = 1 - i; dV[i] = (EL - V[i] - g[i] * P[j] * (V[i] - E[j]) + RI) / taum; }
        for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
          P[i] += dt * (Math.E * Pmax * z[i] * (1 - P[i]) - P[i]) / taus;
          z[i] += dt * (-z[i] / taus);
        }
        for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
          const Vn = V[i] + dt * dV[i];
          if (Vn >= Vth) {
            const frac = (Vth - V[i]) / (Vn - V[i]), ts = t + frac * dt;
            V[i] = Vr + (1 - frac) * dt * dV[i]; z[i] = 1; spikes[i].push(ts);
            trace[i][idx] = 20;
            if (i === 1) {
              const s1 = spikes[0];
              if (s1.length >= 2 && ts >= s1[s1.length - 1]) { const a = s1[s1.length - 1], b = s1[s1.length - 2]; phases.push([ts, (ts - a) / (a - b)]); }
            }
          } else { V[i] = Vn; trace[i][idx] = V[i]; }
          while (spikes[i].length && spikes[i][0] < t - phaseWin) spikes[i].shift();
        }
        while (phases.length && phases[0][0] < t - phaseWin) phases.shift();
        t += dt;
      }
      if (t >= nextRateAt) { for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) lastRate[i] = spikes[i].filter(x => x > t - 1000).length; nextRateAt = t + 1000; }
    }
    yield {V, P, trace, idx, spikes, phases, t, win, phaseWin, lastRate, E: [viewof cnType1.value, viewof cnType2.value], g: [viewof cnG12.value, viewof cnG21.value]};
  }
}
cnCanvas = mkCanvas(760, 320)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const st = cnState, c = cnCanvas, fg = exFg(), W = 760, H = 320;
  const col = ["#9467bd", "#17becf"], red = "#d62728", blue = "#1f77b4";
  const Vth = -54, Vr = -80;
  c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  // circuit diagram, left
  const D = {cx: 95, y1: 58, y2: 196, r: 24};
  const drawNeuron = (i, y) => {
    const exc = st.E[i] === 0;
    c.lineWidth = 2.5; c.strokeStyle = col[i];
    c.fillStyle = i === 0 ? "rgba(148,103,189,0.25)" : "rgba(23,190,207,0.25)";
    c.beginPath();
    if (exc) { c.moveTo(D.cx, y - D.r * 1.1); c.lineTo(D.cx + D.r * 1.1, y + D.r * 0.8); c.lineTo(D.cx - D.r * 1.1, y + D.r * 0.8); c.closePath(); }
    else c.arc(D.cx, y, D.r, 0, 2 * Math.PI);
    c.fill(); c.stroke();
    c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`${i + 1}`, D.cx, y + 5);
    c.fillText(exc ? "excitatory" : "inhibitory", D.cx, y + (i === 0 ? -D.r - 12 : D.r + 22));
  };
  // connections: 1 → 2 on the right, 2 → 1 on the left; thickness ∝ strength; red = excitatory, blue = inhibitory
  const drawSyn = (from, to, side) => {
    const gS = st.g[from === 0 ? 0 : 1], exc = st.E[from] === 0, colr = exc ? red : blue;
    const yA = from === 0 ? D.y1 + D.r : D.y2 - D.r, yB = to === 0 ? D.y1 + D.r + 4 : D.y2 - D.r - 4;
    const x = D.cx + side * 18, xc = D.cx + side * 62;
    c.strokeStyle = colr; c.fillStyle = colr; c.lineWidth = Math.max(0.5, 12 * gS);
    c.globalAlpha = gS === 0 ? 0.25 : 1;
    c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(x, yA); c.bezierCurveTo(xc, yA, xc, yB, x, yB); c.stroke();
    // ending: arrowhead for excitatory, filled dot for inhibitory
    const dir = to === 0 ? -1 : 1, tipY = yB + dir * 2;
    if (exc) { c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(x, tipY + dir * 8); c.lineTo(x - 7, tipY - dir * 4); c.lineTo(x + 7, tipY - dir * 4); c.closePath(); c.fill(); }
    else { c.beginPath(); c.arc(x, tipY + dir * 3, 6, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill(); }
    c.globalAlpha = 1;
  };
  drawSyn(0, 1, 1); drawSyn(1, 0, -1);
  drawNeuron(0, D.y1); drawNeuron(1, D.y2);
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`1→2: ${st.g[0].toFixed(2)}   2→1: ${st.g[1].toFixed(2)}`, D.cx, D.y2 + D.r + 48);
  // voltage traces, middle
  const T = {x0: 240, y0: 14, w: 240, h: 220}, n = st.trace[0].length;
  const tx = i => T.x0 + T.w * i / (n - 1), ty = v => T.y0 + T.h * (1 - (v + 85) / (105));
  axisBox(c, T.x0, T.y0, T.w, T.h);
  c.setLineDash([4, 4]); c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(T.x0, ty(Vth)); c.lineTo(T.x0 + T.w, ty(Vth)); c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
  // oscilloscope sweep: the trace stays in place and is overwritten at the cursor
  for (const i of [1, 0]) {
    c.strokeStyle = col[i]; c.lineWidth = 1.5;
    for (const [a, b] of [[0, st.idx], [st.idx + 1, n - 1]]) {
      if (b <= a) continue;
      c.beginPath();
      for (let k = a; k <= b; k++) k === a ? c.moveTo(tx(k), ty(st.trace[i][k])) : c.lineTo(tx(k), ty(st.trace[i][k]));
      c.stroke();
    }
  }
  c.strokeStyle = "#bbb"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(tx(st.idx), T.y0); c.lineTo(tx(st.idx), T.y0 + T.h); c.stroke();
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("V (mV)", T.x0 - 8, T.y0 + T.h / 2 + 5);
  c.fillText(Vth, T.x0 - 8, ty(Vth) + 5); c.fillText(Vr, T.x0 - 8, ty(Vr) + 5); c.fillText("20", T.x0 - 8, ty(20) + 5);
  c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`${st.win} ms sweep · t = ${(st.t / 1000).toFixed(1)} s`, T.x0 + T.w / 2, T.y0 + T.h + 24);
  c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillStyle = col[0]; c.fillText(`neuron 1: ${st.lastRate[0]} spikes/s`, T.x0, T.y0 + T.h + 46);
  c.fillStyle = col[1]; c.fillText(`neuron 2: ${st.lastRate[1]} spikes/s`, T.x0, T.y0 + T.h + 66);
  // phase difference, right
  const Ph = {x0: 535, y0: 14, w: 215, h: 215};
  const px = tt => Ph.x0 + Ph.w * (1 - (st.t - tt) / st.phaseWin), py = f => Ph.y0 + Ph.h * (1 - f);
  axisBox(c, Ph.x0, Ph.y0, Ph.w, Ph.h);
  c.setLineDash([4, 4]); c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(Ph.x0, py(0.5)); c.lineTo(Ph.x0 + Ph.w, py(0.5)); c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
  c.fillStyle = fg;
  for (const [tt, f] of st.phases) { if (f >= 0 && f <= 1) { c.beginPath(); c.arc(px(tt), py(f), 2.2, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill(); } }
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("1", Ph.x0 - 6, py(1) + 5); c.fillText("½", Ph.x0 - 6, py(0.5) + 5); c.fillText("0", Ph.x0 - 6, py(0) + 5);
  c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText(`time, last ${st.phaseWin / 1000} s`, Ph.x0 + Ph.w / 2, Ph.y0 + Ph.h + 24);
  c.fillText("0: with 1's spike · ½: halfway", Ph.x0 + Ph.w / 2, Ph.y0 + Ph.h + 44);
  c.save(); c.translate(Ph.x0 - 36, Ph.y0 + Ph.h / 2); c.rotate(-Math.PI / 2); c.fillText("spike phase of neuron 2", 0, 0); c.restore();
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Reading the figure

The diagram on the left is the circuit. Neuron 1 is at the top and neuron 2
at the bottom, each drawn as a triangle if it makes excitatory synapses and
as a circle if it makes inhibitory ones. The connection from 1 to 2 runs
down the right side and the one from 2 to 1 up the left side. Each is red
for excitatory and blue for inhibitory, ends in an arrowhead or a dot
accordingly, and its thickness follows the strength slider. The two numbers
under the diagram repeat the strengths.

The middle panel shows 200 milliseconds of both membrane potentials,
neuron 1 in purple and neuron 2 in teal, with spikes drawn as vertical
strokes to 20 mV. It works like an oscilloscope: the trace stays where it
is and a grey cursor sweeps across, overwriting it, so your eye can rest on
the part that has already been drawn. The dashed line is the threshold. The
two numbers below are the firing rates, updated once per simulated second.

The panel on the right is the one to watch. Every time neuron 2 fires, a dot
records when in neuron 1's cycle it did so: 0 means at the same moment as
neuron 1's last spike, ½ means exactly halfway between two spikes of neuron
1, and values near 1 mean just before neuron 1's next spike. If the two
neurons fire in synchrony the dots sit at 0 or 1, which are the same thing.
If they alternate, the dots sit at ½. The panel scrolls over the last five
seconds, so you can see the phase settle from wherever the random start
put it. At the slow setting a 200 ms sweep takes a second or two of real
time; normal is about twice as fast and fast about eight times, which is
useful for the phase panel, where it can take several simulated seconds
for the dots to settle. Pause freezes everything.

## Things to try

Start with the defaults: two inhibitory neurons, both strengths 0.2, and a
synaptic time constant of 10 ms. After the random start, the dots in the
phase panel drift to 0 or 1 within a second or two of simulated time, which
is quicker to watch at the fast setting, and the traces fall on top of each
other. Two neurons that do nothing but inhibit each other fire
in perfect synchrony. The mechanism is in the traces: when one neuron
fires, the other receives an inhibitory current that delays its next spike,
and the delay is longer the closer to threshold the receiver was. The
neuron that was ahead is held back more than the one that was behind, and
the gap closes.

Make both neurons excitatory. Now the dots settle near ½, typically
between 0.4 and 0.6: the neurons alternate. The argument runs the other way round. Excitation shortly after a
neuron's own spike, when it sits at the reset, does little, while excitation
close to threshold triggers a spike immediately. The neuron that is behind
is advanced more than the one ahead, and the gap opens until the two are as
far apart as they can be. Van Vreeswijk, Abbott and Ermentrout (1994) made
this precise, and their title says it all: when inhibition, not excitation,
synchronises neural firing.

The synaptic time constant decides which of these two stories holds. Go back
to two inhibitory neurons and set $\tau_s$ to 3 ms. The dots move to ½:
fast inhibition makes the neurons alternate, not synchronise. The reason is
that the argument above assumed the inhibition is still present when the
receiving neuron gets close to threshold, which requires the synapse to
outlast a good part of the period. At 3 ms it has worn off before it can do
its job. In the gamma models cited at the top, the inhibitory synapses have
time constants around 10 ms, and the oscillation period is set by this
number, which is why the rhythm sits where it does.

Try a mixed pair, one excitatory and one inhibitory, with equal strengths.
After a second of drifting the dots settle at a fixed phase between the two
extremes, and the two neurons fire at the same rate even though one is
being excited and the other inhibited. This pair is the smallest version of
the pyramidal-interneuron loop that generates gamma in the cortex. Make the
excitatory synapse stronger than the inhibitory one and the lock breaks in
an instructive way: the inhibitory neuron, which is being excited, fires two
or three times per cycle of its partner, and the dots fall into several
bands instead of one.

Then set one of the strengths to zero. With a one-way connection the
receiver speeds up or slows down, depending on the sign, but at these
strengths it does not lock to the sender: the dots form diagonal bands that
drift through the panel, which is what two independent oscillators with
slightly different periods look like. Locking needs the influence to go both
ways, or a much stronger synapse. Finally, go back to the two inhibitory
neurons and raise the drive to 40 mV. The rates roughly double, to about
130 spikes per second, and the pair still locks, but no longer in exact
synchrony: the dots settle a little below 1, with one neuron leading the
other by a few percent of the cycle. The period is now short compared with
$\tau_s$, and the lock is on its way to breaking. Shorten $\tau_s$ at this
drive and it does.

This page follows the exercise on synaptic coupling in Dayan and Abbott
(2001, chapter 5), which in turn is based on van Vreeswijk et al. (1994).
